message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and ensure safe, habitable living conditions. Below is an overview of key tenant rights under Texas law (Texas Property Code, Chapter 24) and related statutes: | Category | Key Rights | Practical Implications | |----------|------------|------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit, two months for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | • Keep records of move‑in condition; take photos or videos. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, and pest control.
• Must keep premises in good repair and free from health hazards. | • Report problems promptly; keep written records. | | **Repair & Deduct / Rent Withholding** | • If landlord fails to fix major repairs, tenant may pay the cost and deduct from rent, or withhold rent until repaired. | • Document repairs requested and responses. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice (usually 24 hours) except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of entries. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For nonpayment: 3‑day notice to pay or vacate.
• For lease termination: 30‑day notice if lease is month‑to‑month. | • Provide written notice; keep copies. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Protected classes: race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, etc. | • Landlords cannot refuse or discriminate based on these factors. | | **Eviction Process** | • Must follow court procedure; unlawful eviction (e.g., “self‑eviction” or “no‑court” eviction) is illegal. | • Seek legal counsel if facing eviction. | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease must be in writing for >1 year; must include rent amount, security deposit, lease term, and contact info. | • Verify lease terms before signing. | | **Rent Increases** | • No limit on rent increase for month‑to‑month leases; must give 30‑day notice. | • Plan for potential increases. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Tenant may sublet or assign with landlord’s consent; landlord cannot unreasonably deny. | • Get written permission. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide hot water, heat, and electricity unless otherwise agreed. | • Check utility responsibilities in lease. | | **Landlord’s Right to Enter** | • 24‑hour notice required for non‑emergency visits. | • Keep a log of entries. | | **Legal Remedies** | • Tenants can sue for breach of habitability, unlawful eviction, or discrimination. | • Keep documentation for evidence. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written communication, and receipts help prove your case. 2. **Know the Law** – Familiarize yourself with Texas Property Code § 24.1–24.12 and local ordinances. 3. **Use Written Notices** – Send notices via certified mail or email with read receipt. 4. **Seek Legal Aid** – If you face eviction or disputes, consult a tenant‑rights organization or attorney. ### Resources - **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** – Provides consumer guides and complaint forms. - **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs** – Offers resources on fair housing. - **Local Tenant‑Rights Groups** – Many cities have nonprofits that offer legal clinics. If you have a specific situation (e.g., landlord refusing to make repairs, dispute over security deposit, or facing eviction), let me know and I can provide more tailored guidance or draft a letter to your landlord.
